title: The C file mode that erases your file instantly
description:
Opening a file with "w" in C truncates it to zero length the instant fopen succeeds -- before fprintf writes a single byte. If your program crashes first, the old data is just gone. Here's how to pick between "w" and "a" on purpose so you never wipe a file by accident.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/08-file-io/

#Shorts

beats.narration: You open a file in write mode. Your program crashes before it writes anything. The file is now empty. Not corrupted. Empty.
Here's why. This opens the file with the w flag. The moment fopen succeeds, the old contents are truncated to zero length, before fprintf ever runs.
The lesson says it plainly. Modes w and w plus silently erase any existing content the moment fopen succeeds.

display.heading: Straight from the lesson
display.subheading: "w" erases existing content the moment fopen succeeds

beats.narration: So pick the mode on purpose. Use w when you truly want a fresh file. Reach for a, append mode, when you want to keep what's already there.
Before every fopen in write mode, ask one question. Am I replacing this file, or adding to it? The wrong letter wipes the whole thing.
Full breakdown of every file mode is in the C Mastery Path lesson on File I/O.
